prompt: On demand, what does `SELECT * FROM orders LIMIT 10` cost compared with `SELECT * FROM orders`?
hint: The page has a sentence about `LIMIT`.

choices.text: A tenth of a cent less
choices.why: There is no discount for returning fewer rows.

choices.text: The same
choices.why: Right. Both read every column of every row.

choices.text: Only the bytes of the ten rows returned
choices.why: The bill follows what was read, not what was returned.

choices.text: Nothing, because small results come from the cache
choices.why: The cache answers a query seen before on unchanged tables, whatever its size.

prompt: A query reads 3,000,000 bytes from `orders` and 200 bytes from `stores`. How many bytes does on demand bill?
hint: Each table referenced is billed for at least 10 MB, and a MB is 2^20 bytes.

prompt: A partition filter cuts a query on Quitanda's orders from 9,960,944 bytes to 130,872. What happens to its on-demand bill?
hint: Both numbers are under one threshold.

choices.text: It falls by a factor of about seventy-six
choices.why: It would, without the minimum; both are billed as 10,485,760 bytes.

choices.text: It rises, because a filter is extra work for the slots
choices.why: On demand charges for bytes, not for work.

choices.text: Nothing changes: both are billed at the 10 MB minimum
choices.why: Right. Reading less than 10 MB saves nothing.

choices.text: It becomes free
choices.why: Only failed and cached queries cost nothing.

prompt: An analyst cancels a `SELECT *` over a 2 TiB table after forty seconds, when it has nearly finished. What may it cost?
hint: Cancelling is not a refund.

choices.text: Nothing, because cancelled queries are like failed ones
choices.why: A failed query costs nothing; a cancelled one may be charged up to its full cost.

choices.text: Up to its full cost, 22.50 USD
choices.why: Right. A query that has read the table has been billed for it.

choices.text: Forty seconds of slot time
choices.why: On demand does not bill time at all.

choices.text: Exactly the 10 MB minimum
choices.why: The minimum is a floor, not what a cancelled query pays.

prompt: What is a slot-hour?
hint: The page defines a slot in two words.

choices.text: One virtual CPU used for one hour
choices.why: Right. Capacity pricing bills that, whatever the queries read.

choices.text: A TiB read by one query in an hour
choices.why: That mixes the two models; slots do not bill bytes.

choices.text: An hour in which a reservation answered at least one query
choices.why: Slots are billed by the second and by the slot, not by busy hours.

choices.text: A node of a BigQuery cluster, rented for an hour
choices.why: BigQuery has no clusters or nodes to rent.

prompt: Match each edition to its pay-as-you-go price per slot-hour in southamerica-east1.
hint: One price on the right is a commitment.

prompt: Quitanda wants a one-year commitment on Standard edition to cut its slot price. What does the pricing page say?
hint: Read which editions commitments are sold for.

choices.text: It takes a fifth off, as for Enterprise
choices.why: That is Enterprise's one-year discount; Standard has no commitments.

choices.text: It needs at least 100 slots
choices.why: Commitments start at 50 slots, and not on Standard.

choices.text: Commitments are only for Enterprise and Enterprise Plus
choices.why: Right. Standard is pay-as-you-go and nothing else.

choices.text: It is the default after a month of use
choices.why: Nothing becomes a commitment by itself; a commitment is bought.

prompt: A project has no reservation assignment. How are its queries billed?
hint: A reservation reaches a project only through an assignment.

choices.text: On demand
choices.why: Right. That is the default for any project.

choices.text: On the organisation's largest reservation
choices.why: Without an assignment, no reservation serves it.

choices.text: At Standard edition prices, per slot-hour
choices.why: Standard is a reservation's edition too; with none, the project pays per byte.

choices.text: They are refused until one is made
choices.why: BigQuery runs them on demand without any setup.

prompt: In the model of this lesson, a query needs 10 slots for 6 seconds and arrives alone, without fluid scaling. How many slot-seconds is it billed?
hint: Round the slots up to a step of 50, and the time up to the minimum.

prompt: Why did the store dashboard cost 250 times its work on an autoscaled reservation, and the nightly transformation nothing extra?
hint: Compare each workload with the two rounding rules.

choices.text: The dashboard ran on Standard and the transformation on Enterprise
choices.why: Both were priced at Enterprise's 0.093.

choices.text: Its queries were small and short, so the steps of 50 and the minute dominated
choices.why: Right. 400 slots for two minutes is already a whole step and over a minute.

choices.text: The transformation ran at night, when slots are cheaper
choices.why: The page has no time-of-day price.

choices.text: Dashboards are billed by the bytes they read
choices.why: On a reservation nothing is billed by bytes.

prompt: What does a reservation's baseline cost when no query is running?
hint: The autoscaler only adds slots above it.

choices.text: Nothing, since the autoscaler releases it
choices.why: The autoscaler adds and removes only slots above the baseline.

choices.text: Its slots, every hour, used or not
choices.why: Right. The baseline is the floor you pay for.

choices.text: Half price, as idle capacity
choices.why: There is no idle discount; idle slots may be lent, not discounted.

choices.text: The one-minute minimum, once a day
choices.why: The minute applies to scaled slots; the baseline is paid for all the time.

prompt: At the Enterprise Plus pay-as-you-go price, how many slot-hours can a TiB of queries use before slots cost more than on demand? Round to a whole number.
hint: 11.25 divided by the slot-hour price.

prompt: A workload uses 300 slot-hours for every TiB it reads. Which is cheaper for it?
hint: Compare 300 with the ties: 181, 121 and 73.

choices.text: Standard, the cheapest slot
choices.why: Even Standard's tie is 181, below 300.

choices.text: On demand
choices.why: Right. It needs more compute per byte than any edition's tie.

choices.text: A three-year Enterprise commitment
choices.why: A commitment pays for every hour; it wins only on slots kept busy.

choices.text: Enterprise Plus, for its higher tie
choices.why: Its tie is the lowest, 73, so it loses soonest.

prompt: Why did both 50-slot commitments lose to every other option for Quitanda's two workloads?
hint: How many slot-hours does a commitment buy in a month?

choices.text: Commitments only apply to storage
choices.why: The page says capacity does not cover storage at all.

choices.text: They pay for 36,500 slot-hours a month and the workloads used 600 and 2,500
choices.why: Right. A commitment wins only on slots that stay busy.

choices.text: Their price per slot-hour is higher than pay-as-you-go
choices.why: It is lower, 0.0744 and 0.0558 against 0.093.

choices.text: They cannot be used in São Paulo
choices.why: The page prices them for southamerica-east1.

prompt: Where does a real project find the bytes billed and the slot time of each query it ran?
hint: A view, one row per job.

choices.text: In `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLE_STORAGE`
choices.why: That view is about stored bytes, lesson 13.

choices.text: In DuckDB's plan
choices.why: DuckDB has no slots and bills nothing.

choices.text: In `INFORMATION_SCHEMA.JOBS`
choices.why: Right. `total_bytes_billed` and `total_slot_ms`.

choices.text: Only on the monthly invoice, as a total
choices.why: The invoice totals what the jobs view itemises.

prompt: What does BigQuery do with a query that would take the project past its custom quota for the day?
hint: A quota acts before the bill.

choices.text: Runs it and sends an e-mail
choices.why: That is what a billing budget does, after the money is spent.

choices.text: Refuses it with an error
choices.why: Right. And the quota resets at midnight Pacific time.

choices.text: Moves it to a reservation, if the project has one available
choices.why: A quota does not change a query's pricing model.

choices.text: Runs it on fewer slots, more slowly
choices.why: That is what a reservation's maximum does.

prompt: A reservation is capped with `--autoscale_max_slots=200` and a query needs 400 slots. What happens?
hint: The maximum caps speed as well as cost.

choices.text: It fails, like a query over its quota
choices.why: That is the quota's behaviour; a reservation makes it wait.

choices.text: The reservation goes over 200 for that one query
choices.why: The maximum is never exceeded.

choices.text: It runs on 200 slots and takes longer
choices.why: Right. Slower, never refused.

choices.text: It is sent to on demand to finish
choices.why: A project assigned to a reservation does not fall back by itself.

prompt: Quitanda sets a project quota of 1 TiB a day for its analysts. Their busiest day last month read 1.6 TiB. What does this quota risk?
hint: A quota does not know which query matters.

choices.text: Nothing, since the free TiB covers it
choices.why: The free TiB is a month's, not a day's, and does not raise a quota.

choices.text: A bill above 11.25 USD that day
choices.why: The quota is precisely what keeps the day under that.

choices.text: Legitimate queries failing on heavy days, as if the analysts had caused an outage themselves
choices.why: Right. Set it from a heavy day, with room above.

choices.text: Queries slowing down
choices.why: Slowness is a reservation's maximum; a quota refuses.

prompt: Put the on-demand bill for one query in the order the rules apply.
hint: The price comes last.
items: Count the logical bytes of each referenced column, in each table
Raise each table to at least 10 MB
Round the total up to the next MB

prompt: Which of these numbers in this lesson came out of a measurement here, rather than from the pricing page, the documentation or a stated assumption? Choose all that apply.
hint: Only DuckDB measured anything, on lesson 13's table.

choices.text: `total_cents` is 9,960,944 bytes over the whole table
choices.why: Yes. DuckDB counted the rows.

choices.text: One day of `total_cents` is 130,872 bytes
choices.why: Yes, the same query.

choices.text: The analysts use 600 slot-hours a month
choices.why: A stated assumption; nothing here has slots.

choices.text: The autoscaler adds slots in steps of 50
choices.why: From Google's documentation, applied by a model.

choices.text: An Enterprise slot-hour is 0.093 USD
choices.why: The pricing page, read on 2026-10-30.

prompt: A new team at Quitanda runs a dashboard of hundreds of thousands of tiny queries a month. Which model fits it best, by this lesson's arithmetic?
hint: Price the same queries both ways: 10 MB each, or 50 slots for a minute each.

choices.text: On demand: 100,000 fit in the free TiB
choices.why: Right. On slots, the rounding multiplies the work.

choices.text: An autoscaled Enterprise reservation
choices.why: Each small query pays for 50 slots and a minute.

choices.text: A 3-year commitment of 50 slots
choices.why: 2,036.70 USD a month for work on demand gives away.

choices.text: Enterprise Plus
choices.why: The dearest slot, with the lowest tie.
